column4: The ceremony is identifiable in 1 and 2. The exact numbered day cannot be verified here, and the year reading adds an unsupported time unit. The three other answers invent an emperor in this phrase.
The first leaves the judgment largely in classical wording. Choice 2 changes individual litigants into households and omits the officials.
Both fluent paraphrases preserve the cautions about speech and deportment.
The natural question is explicit in 2. The extraneous syllable in 3 damages an otherwise clear question.
Choice 0 gives the first two contrasts but loses private reputation. Choices 1 and 3 confuse itinerant office-seeking with eunuchs.
Choice 1 supplies a coherent biographical gloss. Choice 0 attributes the lineage to everyone in the heading.
Both fluent choices preserve the sufferers' view that their punishment was just.
Choice 0 works as a terse calendar entry. Choice 1 substitutes a numbered day unverifiable here. Choice 2 destroys the sexagenary day.
The complete simile and participants survive in the first two. Choice 2 corrupts the personal name.
Choice 1 conveys the uprising and reversal. The last two omit what happened in Yingchuan.
Choice 0 includes extraneous material about a pearl. Choice 1 explains why the crossing was impossible.
A banquet is not a sacrifice. Choice 3 gives a reasonable ritual explanation but specifies feudal lords without support inside this sentence.
The first turns delight into rising or flourishing. The other two retain the report and appointment.
Only 0 gives the voice of the unseen daughter. Choice 2 makes her the speaker reporting another person's disappearance.
The exact amount and jurisdiction survive in 0. Choice 2 is unchanged classical wording. A numbered date alone cannot be checked.
The fluent choices retain the people, beneficiary and commemorative purpose.
The first invents a later speaker. Choice 2 identifies the empress and states what to report to whom.
Both alternatives recover the polarity and mania. Floating pulse in 1 and the added heat in 2 interpret details beyond the visible clause.
Choice 1 turns the taking of Daizhou into replacing a prefecture. Choice 2 damages the military office.
Choice 0 keeps the religious return, service and destination. The final choice confuses return with rebellion and negates form incorrectly.
The last two retain the elapsed months, end of danger and intention to depart.
Choice 0 interprets the prison origin and both offices. Choice 2 changes a criminal to a commoner.
The first has a corrupted posthumous-title glyph. The middle pair lose the verb of death. Choice 3 changes the day to a year.
Choice 1 is fluent. The concise bulletin in 2 preserves all places and floods. Choice 3 loses the river's predicate.
Choice 2 preserves the hundreds of paces and makes audibility clear. Choice 0 converts the measure to a different distance.
The first and last give transformation instead of an alternate name. Choice 2 hedges the first identification.
Choice 1 preserves the name, courtesy name and origin without duplicating the heading.
Choice 0 retains general, location and enemy centre. Choice 1 corrupts the proper names. Choice 3 reproduces the classical source.
The two complete similes preserve the comparison to patterned silk.
Choice 0 gives the commander, attack and both deaths. Choice 1 leaves the relation of the general to Xuan unclear. The last three damage the second name.
Both concise biographical formats are acceptable. Choice 0 corrupts the courtesy name and 4 the place.
The original prescribes placing a thick fence on the north side. Facing north is a different instruction.
